articles.title: In 2020, Atlanta began filling Bellwood Quarry with 9.1 billion litres of water, creating an emergency reserve that extended the city’s backup supply from 3–5 days to a month or more
articles.summary: Explore how Atlanta's Bellwood Quarry has evolved from a historical granite pit into a vital emergency water reserve, ensuring the city can sustain its water supply for up to 90 days in times of crisis.
articles.body: The majority of people only consider city water when something goes wrong. Water emerges from the tap when you turn it on, while the storage tanks, pipes and pumps remain out of sight. But Atlanta has always had a subtle weakness. Before the Water Supply Program, Atlanta had about three days of emergency raw-water reserves. The completed system expanded that reserve to more than 30 days, according to PC Construction project. The reservoir can hold 2.4 billion U.S. gallons, or about 9.1 billion litres, the Department of Watershed Management said.The fix was a hole in the earth. In 2020, Atlanta began filling Bellwood Quarry, a century-old granite pit just west of downtown, with river water. The reservoir holds some 2.4 billion US gallons or nearly 9.1 billion litres, the Department of Watershed Management said. The reserve was designed to provide more than 30 days of emergency raw water and potentially up to 90 days with conservation measures. It gives Atlanta a substantial buffer if its normal water supply is disrupted.Granitic pit to reservoirBellwood is no new hole. The site was quarried for well over a century and part of the granite used in paving construction across the city. When the mining was completed, the quarry was a pit about 400 feet deep, or 120 metres. Atlanta bought the site in 2006 to convert it for raw water storage.Construction of the Water Supply Program began in September 2016. Water began flowing into Bellwood Quarry on April 17, 2020, and the program was completed in December 2020. The converted quarry provides approximately 2.4 billion gallons of raw-water storage. Quarries can offer potential sites for water storage because excavation has already created a large basin. In August 2025, Winder and Auburn announced plans to convert a former quarry in Auburn into a one-billion-gallon reservoir, according to the City of Winder.Beneath the city, tunnelsThe river and the quarry are connected via tunnels of solid rock. The construction, according to contractor Clark Construction, is to connect the quarry to the Hemphill pump station and to a site adjacent to the Chattahoochee. One segment is a tunnel through solid rock 10.5 feet wide and eventually extended to about 15,000 feet. At the river end, a 30-foot-square, 350-foot-deep shaft functioned as the point of egress for the boring machine. The project increased Atlanta’s water storage capacity approximately tenfold and received Engineering News-Record Best Project recognition in 2020. The system is bi-directional. Raw water is piped from the river down the tunnel into the quarry and is used untreated. In an emergency, it flows via the tunnel to the Hemphill Water Treatment Plant, is cleansed and sent out to taps like any other supply.What it means for AtlantaAtlanta’s approximately $320 million Water Supply Program was completed in December 2020. The quarry is the centrepiece of Westside Park, a 280-acre green space that the city identifies as Atlanta’s largest park. Visitors should not expect a swimming lake. The place is a restricted drinking water reservoir, and the government restricts any recreational use due to the potential for pollution. Atlanta’s Department of Watershed Management warns that active pumps can pull a person underwater and into the pumping system. Visitors must stay out of the restricted reservoir area and away from the pumps; swimming, boating and other recreational activities are prohibited.And it is worth being explicit, too, about what the reserve is for. The quarry is just buying time. If the river were filthy, or a drought decreased flows to unsafe levels, or the intake collapsed, Atlanta would no longer be counting its safety margin in days. It would have weeks, and that is typically enough to set in motion emergency choices and repair and rationing measures. The conversion gives Atlanta an additional buffer against interruptions to its normal water supply. The former granite quarry now serves as an emergency raw-water reservoir that can provide time for the city to respond when its usual supply is disrupted.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1979, a Florida woman spent a week in a 50-foot eagle’s nest; her stunt helped fund a raptor centre that had released 620+ rehabilitated bald eagles by 2019
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable journey of Doris Mager, who lived in a 50-foot eagle's nest to raise funds for a bird rehabilitation center that has helped over 620 bald eagles. Learn how her actions contributed to the conservation of this iconic species and the impact of the Audubon Centre for Birds of Prey.
articles.body: The bald eagle faced significant challenges throughout the United States in the early 1970s. The national bird was in a sharp decline due to habitat destruction, DDT, and illegal shooting; in 1973, Florida recorded just 88 active nests. There was no designated location for ill and injured birds of prey in Central Florida at the time, so anyone who spotted an injured hawk, owl, or eagle had virtually nowhere to send it.That gap was what put Doris Mager in a tree. Mager, a gift shop manager at the Florida Audubon Society's office in Maitland, had spent years nursing injured raptors and in June 1979 she climbed 50 feet into an abandoned eagle's nest to raise money and attention for a proper rehabilitation centre. She was there a week. The Audubon Center for Birds of Prey opened on October 19, 1979. By its 40th anniversary in 2019, it had released more than 620 rehabilitated bald eagles into the wild, according to Audubon’s anniversary report.How it startedMager began her rescue efforts in 1963, when a visitor brought a red-tailed hawk with an infected foot into the gift shop. She took the bird home, placed its foot in warm water and Epsom salt and released it a month later. She was no expert and thus sought instruction from raptor specialist John Hamlet. Word got out, and additional injured birds came in; at one point, she had seven eagles in her backyard. By the 1970s, both Mager and Audubon Florida could see that a dedicated facility was needed. Some sizeable donations had come in, but funding still fell short. Then she remembered a story about a couple in British Columbia who had spent a night in an eagle’s nest.A week in the treetopsMager thought, as she subsequently described it, that residing in an eagle's nest to collect money would be the best trick possible. She selected a nest high in a dead longleaf pine. Her greatest worry was if they’d let her. Disturbing a bird’s nest is banned in many circumstances, especially if the species is endangered. The US Fish and Wildlife Service said it did not support the proposal but would not stop her.Some of Mager’s friends were experienced tree climbers, so they helped install a ladder and lightning rods and build a pulley system to transport food, water and waste. Mager began her weeklong stay on June 14, 1979. By the morning of June 15, she had completed her first night in the nest. Audubon’s account notes that she was never left alone during the stay. Friends, colleagues and volunteers gathered under the tree to support the fundraiser. About 50 came to see her every day, including journalists, and on one wet day a string of cars got stranded in the mud on the way to the location. She remembered the mist coming off Lake Harney that first morning. She remembered the tree swaying so fiercely she had to hold on fast. The place she helped create has had a long career since.What the centre has doneBy 2019, the centre was taking in over 700 wounded or orphaned raptors per year and had released over 250 of them in the year prior. Birds who survive but can’t be released become educational ambassadors. Audubon’s 2019 report said more than 400 volunteers monitored over 700 eagle nests in Florida, while the centre’s staff investigated causes of illness and death in raptors, including pesticide exposure, microplastics and lead poisoning.In the lower 48 states, bald eagle numbers recovered from an estimated 417 breeding pairs in 1963 to 9,789 by 2007. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service removed the species from the federal list of threatened and endangered wildlife in the lower 48 states in 2007, although bald eagles remain protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. By 2019, Florida had about 1,500 nesting pairs. Habitat protections and the DDT ban contributed to the recovery, and Charles Lee of Audubon Florida told Audubon that a significant percentage of the state’s eagles descended from rehabilitated birds. Mager continued her conservation work. In 1981, she travelled around the country in a van with her raptors, visiting schools and speaking to community groups. She later founded a conservation nonprofit called Save Our American Raptors. She turned 95 in 2019.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Feminists Lied’ tour aims to challenge abortion, feminism narratives on college campuses
articles.summary: Turning Point USA and Students for Life of America launched the "Feminists Lied: Prove Me Wrong" tour, continuing Charlie Kirk's legacy on campuses.
articles.body: Just over a year after the assassination of Turning Point USA (TPUSA) founder Charlie Kirk, the organization is teaming up with Students for Life of America (SFLA) to launch a tour focused on discussing feminism and abortion with college students. The tour will be the first-ever partnership between the two groups. The tour, which is being called "Feminists Lied: Prove Me Wrong," is kicking off on Tuesday with eight events scheduled at campuses across the country, including University of North Texas, Grand Valley State University, University of Cincinnati, Boise State University, University of New Mexico, University of Arizona, Southern Oregon University and University of Washington. The organizations say that the campus tour is aimed at challenging "the claim that feminism and 'reproductive rights' have helped women more than they’ve harmed them." "There’s a lot of young women who have bought the lies of the second wave and third wave of feminism, and are actually walking around hurt on college campuses unaware of where the pro-life movement really stands with women, all that we do to serve women and families facing unplanned pregnancies and beyond," SFLA President Kristan Hawkins told Fox News Digital. INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES Hawkins is set to speak at the events and ask the students a fundamental question at the heart of the debate topic: "Have women been told the truth about career, equality, empowerment and motherhood?" "If men do not have to sacrifice their children in order to succeed, why should women?" Hawkins said in a statement announcing the tour. "A society that values women should treat motherhood as an essential contribution worthy of honor, not a liability. Students deserve to hear that case, and we are going to make it on their campuses." The "Feminists Lied: Prove Me Wrong" events will mirror Kirk’s famous "Prove Me Wrong" sessions during which he would debate college students and allow them to ask questions about various controversial topics. He was in the middle of one of these events on Sept. 10, 2025, when he was shot and killed. Since his death, TPUSA has kept Kirk's spirit alive through the Pick Up the Mic initiative, bringing debates and open conversations with a full roster of speakers, including Hawkins. "Charlie and I were friends, and so it means a great deal to me to be on campuses with his chapters at Turning Point and to really continue doing the work that he set out to do," Hawkins told Fox News Digital. OPINION: I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT. OUR PROFESSION SHOULD FINISH WHAT CHARLIE KIRK STARTED Hawkins said that prior to Kirk's death, the two had been trading stories and photos of their visits to various college campuses where they would speak with students, and she believes it is "extremely important that we continue this free speech work" that Kirk started. Hawkins rejected criticism of college visits like hers as a form of "rage bait," saying that they are not meant to merely incite division and spark anger, but rather to change minds in meaningful ways. "These videos, these conversations that we're having, not only do they change [the] minds of the 100-plus students who are gathered who can actually hear the conversation happening in real time, they change tens of thousands of minds of young people online," Hawkins said. Hawkins told Fox News Digital that she has seen the results of these conversations for herself in real life. She said that she has held children whose mothers were thinking about getting an abortion and changed their minds after watching videos of debates online. "There's not a doubt in my mind that these conversations are important for saving lives and changing minds," Hawkins said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Hawkins is no stranger to campus debates. Over the course of 20 years, she has built a national network of Student for Life campus groups across all 50 states. This past spring, she embarked on the "Abortion is Human Sacrifice" tour, which was also aimed at discussing the issue of abortion with college students. Hawkins told Fox News Digital that it doesn't matter whether she is at an Ivy League or a community college campus, the conversations often involve the same arguments from pro-choice advocates. "It really doesn't matter, to be honest with you, if I'm at Harvard or if I'm in a community college or a high school, the questions about abortion are about the exact same, no matter where you go," she said. "You will always get a question about children in foster care, as if a child being in foster care somehow justifies the violence of abortion against a million children a year. You will hear horrific stories about sexual assault and rape, and sometimes these are very deeply personal stories." Ultimately, Hawkins believes that the key to winning over the hearts and minds of those on the other side comes down to the question of "what is inside a woman?" "If what's inside a woman is a meaningless clump of cells that is not a human person, then there is no permission needed for abortion, abortion's fine, abortion is nothing," Hawkins said. "But if what's inside of the woman is unique, all-living human being who is completely unique and unrepeatable, then we need to have a conversation about that human being because all of those things that you hear as a justification for abortion under circumstances, those stop being justifications for harming another member of our human species." While the conversations may have stayed the same, the demographics, according to Hawkins, are changing. She noticed that Gen Z men tend to be more pro-life than millennial men. However, Gen Z women still tend to be pro-choice, according to Hawkins. The pro-life advocate wants to help these young women understand how feminism has failed them. "When I'm on campus today, when I am on campus this semester, a lot of my conversations are going to be towards the women and really addressing the lies that the second wave, the late second-wave feminists, the third-wave feminists, told women, that they needed abortion in order to be free and equal. That that was going to make us happy and responsibility-free, and it hasn't worked and by any measure by looking anxiety rates, depression rates, SSRI use, that hasn't worked," Hawkins told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Young women are increasingly unhappy," she added. "They are not doing okay and we need to back up the conversation and ask the question of ‘why?’"

articles.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case linked to East Africa
articles.summary: A female patient is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.
articles.body:
Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state.

Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests.

The patient is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.

Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified.

Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports .

It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.

The disease has also spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.

On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.

Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers.

The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt.

It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola.

In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths.

articles.title: A 33-year-old California swimmer spent 111 days covering 900 miles of coastline in stages, battling seven-foot waves and polluted water; Catherine Breed has now completed her journey from Oregon to Mexico
articles.summary: For 111 days, Catherine Breed's world was measured in stretches of open water.
articles.body: For 111 days, Catherine Breed's world was measured in stretches of open water. One day brought towering waves, another brought punishing currents, and sometimes the ocean offered little more than exhaustion and uncertainty. Swimming roughly 10 miles a day, the 33-year-old ultra-endurance athlete has now completed a 900-mile journey along California's coastline, turning an extraordinary personal challenge into a broader statement about endurance and ocean conservation.900 miles, one stroke at a timeAccording to The Guardian, Breed began her swim on July 1 at the northern edge of California, close to the Oregon border, with the goal of reaching San Diego in less than four months. Rather than attempting the coastline in one continuous swim, she tackled it in stages, covering about 10 miles on swimming days while a support vessel accompanied her throughout the expedition.As per the report, her team also documented the journey for the World Open Water Swimming Association. Breed slept aboard the support ship between stages and stopped at various points along the coast to participate in events with ocean conservation organisations, adds The Guardian report. Much of the expedition was also shared online, giving viewers a glimpse into the physical demands of an undertaking that stretched across more than 900 miles of Pacific coastline.According to Swimming World report, the scale was dramatically different from Breed's previous endurance swims. She had already crossed the English Channel in 2018 and the North Channel between Northern Ireland and Scotland in 2019, but those iconic open-water crossings were relatively short compared with the sustained demands of swimming down an entire coastline.Seven-foot waves and relentless conditionsThe Guardian report states that Breed encountered waves reaching around seven feet, with rough conditions making sections of the journey feel more like being trapped in a washing machine than moving steadily through the water.Weather added another layer of difficulty. The swim coincided with an unusually intense El Niño season, bringing tropical storms, powerful surf and shifting ocean conditions. A large pulse of warm water, known as a Kelvin wave, also moved northward through the Pacific during the expedition, the report explains.For Breed, the conditions meant fighting currents for much of the journey rather than benefiting from them. The final stretch presented another challenge as she approached Imperial Beach near the US-Mexico border, an area known for severely polluted coastal waters.An environmental message beneath the challengeThe Swimming World states that the difficult final miles underscored one of the central reasons Breed undertook the expedition. "I wanted to prove to myself that I could endure, highlight California's coastline, and inspire more people to conserve the ocean," she said.The swimmer saw the Pacific's sea life and dramatic coastlines, but also plastic waste and polluted water for months. Her journey became a moving portrait of an ecosystem that can be both breathtaking and deeply vulnerable.Breed has also used the swim to encourage more women and girls to spend time in and around the ocean, hoping the expedition will inspire a stronger connection with the water, the report explains.A lifetime in open waterFor the uninitiated, for Breed, the coastline is familiar territory. A former University of California, Berkeley long-distance swimmer and US national team member, she moved into open-water swimming after college through San Francisco's Dolphin Club. Her record already includes a fast swim across Lake Tahoe in 2017, a 25-mile journey from the Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay in 2022 and a demanding 30-mile crossing from the Farallon Islands to the Golden Gate Bridge last year.Images Courtesy: Instagram/catherinebreedYou use AI every day. articles.title: Americans warned about Paris travel after violence, looting and tear gas-filled streets
articles.summary: A tourist described Paris as a war zone as the U.S. Embassy urged Americans in France to avoid protest areas. Curfews have hit Paris, with train closures and flight delays possible.
articles.body: The U.S. Embassy in France is warning Americans to steer clear of violent protests as unrest sparked curfews and raised concerns about travel disruptions across the country. The riots — fueled by a range of grievances, including rising living costs and mass migration — have been reported across France, with protests reported in cities including Paris, Lille and Lyon. Authorities have imposed localized curfews as a result. The embassy said in a Monday statement that partial curfews had been introduced in several French cities, with additional restrictions possible. MCDONALD'S RANSACKED AND WRECKED AS STORES, RESTAURANTS SUFFER FROM VIOLENCE AND RIOTING "Following the October 17 protests that turned violent, media report the Prime Minister’s office introduced partial curfews for Monday, October 19 and Tuesday, October 20 in several cities across France, including Lille," the embassy said. "Media report more curfews may follow for parts of Paris and in prefectures across the country, and that scattered protests could continue." In Paris, authorities also imposed overnight curfews in areas including Place de la République and the Les Halles Shopping District, according to The Associated Press (AP). Riot police deployed tear gas across the streets near Place de la République in an attempt to disperse crowds during the escalating street battles, the same source reported. ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT The gas quickly mixed with heavy, acrid smoke from torched vehicles and street fires, according to Reuters. The chaos forced Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who was visiting Paris with his children, to evacuate his hotel at Place de la République. "It's like a war zone here." De Boer described the scene to Reuters as "like a war zone" following the intense protests that rocked the French capital on Oct. 17. "It's like a war zone here," De Boer said, according to the Reuters report. TOP TOURIST DESTINATION IN THE WORLD SHUTS DOWN AMID VIOLENT PROTESTS Major tourist attractions have also been impacted. The Louvre Museum in Paris was forced to close Monday after protesters blocked its entrances, Fox News Digital previously reported. Travelers visiting Paris are being advised to avoid popular protest gathering spots, including Place de la République, Place de la Bastille and Place de la Nation, along with major thoroughfares such as Boulevard Voltaire, which are frequently used for demonstrations, according to The Times of London. Outside the capital, Lyon's tourism office at Place Bellecour was vandalized and set ablaze during the Oct. 17 demonstrations, according to city officials. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Visitor services have since been relocated to a temporary facility on the same square. The violence also spread to other French cities, including Limoges, where the historic town hall was set ablaze during the Oct. 17 unrest, according to numerous reports. In Bordeaux, the mayor reported that as many as 100 stores had been looted during the demonstrations, Reuters reported. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Despite the violence, flights to and from Paris have largely continued operating, according to flight data reviewed by Fox News Digital. However, travelers could still face disruptions on the ground, with the embassy advising Americans to check for Metro station closures and other transportation interruptions before heading out. The embassy also urged travelers to confirm flight schedules directly with their airlines and allow extra time to reach their destinations. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Monitor media and local resources for updated information and curfews in your area," the statement added. "Plan alternative routes and allow extra travel time for travel." Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment. articles.title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
articles.summary: Ukraine had accused the US of withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by Washington.
articles.body:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff.

The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed.

Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday.

Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link.

A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps".

The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually.

Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.

Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism

Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC

Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now".

"Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said.

He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia.

Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink.

Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine.

And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war.

"Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.

The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.

Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.

European leaders meanwhile have expressed concern about recent US statements from the US towards Russia.

On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".

"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.

Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".

"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

articles.title: 'Russia is a big machine': Trump says Ukraine 'has to want' to settle war with Putin
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump placed the burden on Ukraine to end the nearly four-year war with Russia, arguing that Moscow's military strength and
articles.body: US President Donald Trump placed the burden on Ukraine to end the nearly four-year war with Russia, arguing that Moscow's military strength and territorial gains leave Kyiv at a disadvantage."Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, signalling that he expects Kyiv to move towards a negotiated settlement even as the fighting continues.Trump pointed to Russia's ability to sustain its military campaign and capture territory, portraying Moscow as having the upper hand in the conflict."Russia is a big machine - they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land," he said.His remarks came as his envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday as Washington continued its efforts to broker an end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.Trump also questioned the value of American assistance to Kyiv, complaining that Washington had spent heavily on supporting Ukraine without receiving anything in return."We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss," he said.The US president also pointed to the deep hostility between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy, suggesting that their personal animosity had become an obstacle to negotiations. He described the hatred between the two leaders as "tremendous".Trump further claimed that European countries were growing weary of the conflict, although European governments have been working to offset any reduction in American military support for Kyiv.Trump eases sanctions pressure on RussiaTrump's push for a settlement comes as his administration has taken steps to ease economic pressure on Moscow, raising questions about whether the shift could strengthen Russia's position even as Washington seeks to end the war.On Friday night, Trump signed an executive order exempting Russia from sanctions under a new measure passed by Congress last month. The decision provides additional economic relief to Moscow at a time when the US is also seeking Russian cooperation to bring down fuel prices.The legislation, named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, was designed to squeeze the financial resources sustaining Russia's war against Ukraine. It also gave Trump additional authority to impose tariffs on countries that continue to trade with Moscow.The White House has broad powers to grant sanctions exemptions under the law. It requires the president to notify Congress if he decides against imposing the restrictions.Trump exercised that authority two days before the sanctions were due to take effect.“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”The order did not explain in detail why lifting the restrictions would serve American interests or spell out the reasoning presented to Congress.The decision marks another shift in Trump's approach to Russia. In recent weeks, he has expressed frustration with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that the strikes have contributed to rising petrol and diesel prices.The administration has sought to ease fuel costs by allowing Russian diesel supplies into US and global markets, despite years of sanctions imposed on Moscow following its invasion of Ukraine.However, the war involving Iran remains the biggest factor restricting fuel supplies, limiting how much relief the Russian measures can deliver.US-Ukraine ties face growing strainThe sanctions waiver adds to mounting tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump's latest remarks suggesting that his administration increasingly expects Ukraine to make concessions to end the conflict.The relationship has also been affected by disruptions to satellite support for Ukrainian drones, raising concerns about Kyiv's ability to sustain its military operations if American assistance weakens further.At the same time, Trump's decision to ease sanctions has drawn criticism from those who argue that reducing economic pressure could give Putin more resources to sustain the war rather than bring him closer to a settlement.The administration's approach reflects its competing priorities. Trump wants to end the fighting, reduce economic pressures at home and limit the cost of continued American involvement. But his willingness to relax restrictions on Moscow has raised questions about the leverage Washington may be giving up in negotiations.For Ukraine, the challenge is to secure an agreement that ends the fighting without sacrificing its territorial integrity or long-term security. Trump's latest comments make clear that he wants Kyiv to move towards a deal, while his assessment of Russia's battlefield advantage suggests he believes Ukraine has limited room to negotiate from strength.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mann hands over Jhota murder probe to CBI
articles.summary: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann hands Parvinder Singh Jhota murder probe to CBI after family demand, ahead of Amit Shah visit; agency to file fresh FIR.
articles.body: Mansa: Punjab govt has decided to hand over investigation into the murder of anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota to CBI, chief minister Bhagwant Mann announced on Tuesday, only hours before Union home minister Amit Shah was to visit the bereaved family in Mansa.At 9.49am, Mann posted on X: “We stand strongly with Parvinder Singh Jhota’s father and the family who are fighting against drugs. Accepting the demand of the family, this case is being handed over to CBI. The fight against drugs is decisive, whatever step has to be taken to make Punjab drug-free will be done.”The decision came as a surprise to many as AAP and Mann have repeatedly accused CBI of working for BJP’s political ambitionsJhota’s father Bhim Singh, an ex-Serviceman, has been seeking a CBI probe into the murder. The family had made it clear it wasn’t happy with the way Punjab Police was handling the probe. On Monday, Bhim Singh had announced that since Punjab govt wasn’t accepting his demand for a CBI investigation, he would raise the issue before Shah during his visit.The ‘action committee’ formed to fight for justice after Jhota’s murder on Oct 13, too, had been demanding a central probe.On Monday, the high-powered govt committee of three women IAS officers met the bereaved family and action committee members for the first time where Bhim Singh and his daughter-in-law Manpreet Kaur reiterated their demand for a CBI investigation. The next morning, the CM announced the CBI probe.The central agency is expected to register a fresh FIR and seek the case records from Punjab Police.Jhota had been relentlessly fighting against those selling drugs, including chemists suspected of illegally selling prescription medicines. articles.title: In 1971, a hijacker vanished with $200,000; in 1980, an 8-year-old found part of the ransom on a Washington riverbank, and a damaged $20 note from the discovery sold for $134,200 at auction in 2026
articles.summary: A worn fragment of a $20 banknote linked to the famous 1971 D.B. Cooper hijacking has sold for $134,200 (£102,800) at an auction in Dallas, Texas.
articles.body: A worn fragment of a $20 banknote linked to the famous 1971 D.B. Cooper hijacking has sold for $134,200 (£102,800) at an auction in Dallas, Texas. The damaged banknote is one of the few pieces of physical evidence ever recovered from the ransom money given to the unidentified hijacker before he parachuted into the wilderness of the Pacific Northwest. According to official sales records published by Heritage Auctions, the 1969-series $20 Federal Reserve Note, with serial number L32796069A, was part of the GACC U.S. Currency Signature Auction held from October 6 to October 9, 2026.Raiden Honaker, Director of U.S. Currency at Heritage Auctions, spoke about the banknote's unusual historical appeal after the sale. "High denominations always garner attention from the most serious collectors, and the $10,000 that led this auction is an extraordinary example that drew a result fitting of a note of this caliber," Honaker said in a press release issued by Heritage Auctions. "The $10,000 and $5,000 Federal Reserve Notes are extraordinary pieces of American monetary history, but what makes this auction particularly exciting is the strength of the material across so many different collecting specialties. From an exceptionally rare fractional currency pair to a surviving piece of the D.B. Cooper ransom, collectors had opportunities to acquire notes with compelling histories and remarkable rarity."Hijacking and the vanishing extortionistThe story behind the banknote began on November 24, 1971, when a passenger using the name Dan Cooper boarded a Northwest Orient Airlines Boeing 727 flight from Portland, Oregon, to Seattle, Washington. According to case records held by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cooper gave a flight attendant a note claiming he had a bomb in his briefcase. After the plane landed in Seattle, he released 36 passengers in exchange for $200,000 in cash. The ransom consisted of 10,000 unrecorded $20 bills and came with four parachutes. Following Cooper's instructions, the plane took off again and headed toward Reno, Nevada. Somewhere between Seattle and Reno, over a remote, heavily forested area of southwestern Washington state, Cooper lowered the plane's rear stairs and jumped into a cold rainstorm at night with the ransom money. Despite a major FBI search known as NORJAK (Northwest Hijacking), federal agents found no trace of Cooper, his parachutes, or the money for nearly a decade.Discovery on Tena Bar riverbankThe mystery took an unexpected turn in February 1980, when eight-year-old Brian Ingram was digging in the sand to build a campfire during a family outing at Tena Bar. The beach lies along the Columbia River near Vancouver, Washington. According to historical records from the FBI, Ingram found three decaying bundles of ransom money buried in the sand. The bundles contained about $5,800. Federal investigators checked the serial numbers on the damaged bills and confirmed that they matched the official list of $20 notes handed to Cooper during the 1971 hijacking. The discovery led to renewed searches along the riverbanks. However, investigators could not determine whether river currents had carried the money to Tena Bar or whether Cooper had buried it there himself. In 1986, federal authorities allowed the Ingram family to keep some of the recovered bills. These notes have appeared at major currency auctions from time to time over the following decades.Market interest and auction resultsThe $134,200 sale shows that public interest in the unsolved case remains strong. The D.B. Cooper hijacking is still the only unsolved skyjacking in commercial aviation history. The $20 note fragment sold by Heritage Auctions has badly damaged edges, water damage, and missing sections. These marks resulted from years of exposure to river sediment before the note was found in 1980. According to official reporting from Heritage Auctions, the D.B. Cooper bill was offered alongside historically important high-denomination banknotes. The auction brought in a total of $8,727,555 from sales of US paper money. The FBI officially ended its active field investigation into the Cooper case in July 2016. The agency redirected its resources to other criminal cases but continues to review physical evidence and serial numbers submitted by members of the public.You use AI every day. articles.title: Steve Buscemi returned to firefighting after 9/11 and backed a charity for his former colleagues; by 2024, it was delivering over 4,200 counselling sessions a year to firefighters and families
articles.summary: Hollywood actor Steve Buscemi had left the New York City Fire Department to pursue acting, but the September 11, 2001, attacks brought him back to the
articles.body: Hollywood actor Steve Buscemi had left the New York City Fire Department to pursue acting, but the September 11, 2001, attacks brought him back to the fire service. The next morning, he returned to Ground Zero, where he joined firefighters searching through the rubble of the World Trade Center. Years later, he continued supporting his former colleagues through Friends of Firefighters, a nonprofit that provides free, confidential mental health services to firefighters and their families.According to an article Steve himself wrote for TIME magazine in September 2021, he had spent four years working at Engine 55 in Lower Manhattan before taking a leave of absence to focus on acting. He had expected to return to firefighting one day. After the attacks, he collected his old gear, got a lift to the disaster site and joined a bucket brigade moving debris. “Seventeen years later, I was,” Buscemi wrote in TIME, referring to his return to the fire service. He described the rubble being passed along the line and recalled the disturbing sight of body bags being carried away.The actor said the dust at Ground Zero was initially treated as a nuisance, even as it clogged masks and made working difficult. He recalled someone warning, “This is probably going to kill us in 20 years.” The long-term consequences of toxic exposure became a major concern for first responders. In his TIME essay, Buscemi wrote that chronic health conditions emerged before the recovery work at the site was even complete. He also noted that many people who worked at Ground Zero continued to face health problems long after the attacks.Why Buscemi returned to his old firehouseBuscemi joined the FDNY in the 1980s. According to TIME magazine, he explained that his father, a New York City sanitation worker, had encouraged him and his brothers to take a civil service test when they turned 18. Buscemi took the Fire Department's test and was assigned to Engine 55. He initially kept his acting ambitions quiet at the firehouse. Eventually, however, balancing firefighting shifts with film and theatre work became difficult, prompting him to take a leave of absence.The connection he had formed with the department remained important to him. In the days following 9/11, he said, he felt a strong sense of belonging among the people working at Ground Zero. He spent less than a week at the site, but said the scale of the tragedy caught up with him after he returned home.Buscemi also wrote that he was already seeing a therapist. Having someone with whom he could sit and process his feelings helped him deal with what had happened. He noted that this kind of support was not something first responders usually received. That experience helped explain why mental health support for firefighters became an issue he continued to speak about.How Friends of Firefighters beganIn his TIME essay, Buscemi credited Nancy Carbone with recognising that firefighters needed a place where they could discuss the emotional impact of 9/11. Carbone, a Brooklyn resident, began visiting firehouses in the aftermath of the attacks to ask how she could help. According to the official Friends of Firefighters website, she founded the organisation in 2001 to provide free, confidential and culturally appropriate mental health and wellness services to active and retired FDNY firefighters and their families.Friends of Firefighters was created to address that gap. It offered a way for firefighters to seek help outside the department, without the fear that their conversations would be reported through official employment channels. The organisation expanded its work beyond individual firefighters to include their spouses, children and other family members.More than 4,200 counselling sessions a yearBy 2024, Friends of Firefighters was delivering more than 4,200 counselling sessions annually, according to its website. The services reach active firefighters, retirees, spouses and children, while maintaining confidentiality and independence from department oversight. That figure is a measure of counselling sessions, not the number of individual people served. The organisation's work includes mental health counselling, peer support and wellness services. Its approach recognises that firefighters may be reluctant to discuss trauma, grief or stress with people who have not experienced the demands of their profession.Buscemi's role in the organisationBuscemi is not the founder of Friends of Firefighters. He supports its work and serves on its advisory council, alongside other public figures and people connected to the fire service. The website lists him as an actor, writer, director and former FDNY firefighter. As reported by Global Heroes, he has helped with fundraising and used his public profile to draw attention to firefighters' experiences. He has also helped tell their stories through documentary projects, including ‘A Good Job: Stories of the FDNY’ and ‘Dust: The Lingering Legacy of 9/11.’ The latter examines the continuing consequences of exposure to hazardous dust at the World Trade Center site.In an interview with Global Heroes, Buscemi described the importance of making sure people do not feel alone in what they are going through. “So many people can feel isolated or that they’re the only ones that are going through this,” he said. “It’s important to know that we’re all going through this together.” He also stressed that the effects of 9/11 did not end when the immediate rescue and recovery work finished.You use AI every day. articles.title: Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey spares death row inmate, citing doubts about evidence
articles.summary: Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey on Tuesday commuted the death sentence of a death-row inmate after a number of former public officials, and the current district attorney, raised doubts about his conviction.
articles.body: Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey on Tuesday commuted the death sentence of a death-row inmate after a number of former public officials, and the current district attorney, raised doubts about his conviction. The Republican governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life in prison without parole. Johnson was convicted of the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. Johnson has long maintained he is innocent. “When presented with Mr. Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death,” Ivey said in a statement. “My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole.” Ivey has overseen 27 executions during her time as governor. She has commuted the death sentence of three death row inmates. Hardy was shot twice in the head while working off-duty security at a hotel. Johnson has maintained he was on the other side of town at the time of the shooting. Ty Alper, one of Toforest Johnson’s attorneys, said they are grateful to Ivey for “diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution.” Alper said the fight to overturn the conviction will continue. “Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” Alper said. There has been a long-running legal effort to win a new trial in the case that has garnered national attention and was the subject of a podcast. Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr, who was elected in 2018, has supported Johnson’s bid for a new trial. Carr wrote in a 2024 court filing that the “evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years.” Carr said in 2024 that credible alibi witnesses place Johnson elsewhere at the time of the crime. He said there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness, a woman who “claimed she overheard Johnson confess to the murder on a three-way phone call on which she was eavesdropping.” The key prosecution witness at Johnson's 1998 trial testified that, while eavesdropping on a phone call, she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the crime. She was paid $5,000 in 2001 for her testimony, and Johnson’s lawyers argue that the state withheld evidence of monetary motivation for the testimony. A number of former judges and prosecutors have joined those seeking a new trial for Johnson amid questions about his conviction more than 20 years ago. Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, former Chief Justices Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers, and several former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials supporting a new trial.

articles.title: Australian billionaire James Packer listed his Los Angeles mansion for about $85 million in 2023; after roughly a year on the market, it sold in 2025 for $60 million
articles.summary: Australian billionaire James Packer parted with his Los Angeles mansion, closing a chapter that drew wide attention across the world of luxury real estate.
articles.body: Australian billionaire James Packer parted with his Los Angeles mansion, closing a chapter that drew wide attention across the world of luxury real estate. Listed in 2023 at around 85 million dollars, the sprawling Beverly Hills estate sold in 2025 for 60 million dollars, well below what its owner first hoped to achieve. The property has twelve bedrooms, eighteen bathrooms, a celebrity past and a lavish entertainment suite, yet it still needed more than a year to find a buyer. Here is how the sale unfolded, what the estate offers, and what Packer did next.Why the James Packer mansion sold for 60 million dollars, not the 85 million he wantedJames Packer first listed the property in September 2023, hoping to achieve about 85 million dollars, which Domain put at roughly 132 million Australian dollars. After more than a year on the market, the estate sold for 60 million dollars (93.5 million Australian dollars). That leaves the final price 25 million dollars, or close to 29 per cent, below the amount first sought. A sold sticker appeared on the online listing on a Monday, bringing the long wait to an end.Inside the twelve-bedroom Beverly Hills estate with a wine cellar, cinema, cigar room and games roomThe home is a three-storey residence, built in 1930, set on a block of 0.76 hectares (1.88 acres) with twelve bedrooms and eighteen bathrooms. Outside, the landscaped grounds hold a pool, a spa and an outdoor dining area with an al fresco kitchen, while two garages complete the practical side of the property. Inside, the entertainment spaces include a cinema room, a fitness room, a cigar room, a wine cellar and a games room fitted with a bar and billiards. Formal living and dining spaces round out the layout, and Domain noted they are ideal for entertaining guests. Taken together, the facilities show why the estate was pitched at the very top of the Los Angeles luxury property market, where buyers expect extensive amenities.Danny DeVito, Jennifer Lopez and Ben Affleck, the star-studded history of this Beverly Hills mansionThe home reportedly has a star-studded history. Danny DeVito and Rhea Perlman owned it from the 1990s, then sold it to developers who rebuilt the residence before it passed to Packer. The property was also leased for a time by Jennifer Lopez and Ben Affleck. Packer was said to have invested in upgrades during his ownership, adding further polish to an address already known for famous former residents. The listing agents were Santiago Arana of The Agency and Jade Mills of Coldwell Banker Realty. Such a pedigree can lift public interest in a property, although in this case it did not prevent a sale well below the original asking price of 85 million dollars.Packer buys the former home of Gigi and Bella Hadid for a reported 110 million dollarsThe deal for the Beverly Hills estate was secured after Packer bought another home in the city. He was reported to have spent 110 million dollars on the former home of supermodels Gigi and Bella Hadid, a purchase made in the same year as the sale of his earlier mansion. articles.title: Washington Post columnist reinstated after being fired over Charlie Kirk posts gloats about receiving back pay
articles.summary: Karen Attiah celebrated her arbitration win against The Washington Post, sharing a Rihanna dance video after being awarded a year's worth of back pay.
articles.body: A columnist took a victory lap Tuesday as The Washington Post was ordered to give her back pay after she challenged her firing last year. "POV: Channeling my inner Rihanna because I won my case against the @washingtonpost — and they owe me a year’s worth of back pay," Karen Attiah wrote on X while sharing a video of her dancing to a Rihanna song. In August, an arbitrator ordered the Post to reinstate her employment and give her back pay, saying the paper "did not have good and sufficient cause" and that it "violated" her labor agreement. WASHINGTON POST ORDERED TO REINSTATE COLUMNIST KAREN ATTIAH AFTER BEING TERMINATED OVER CHARLIE KIRK POSTS "I'm still processing everything, but overall, I am happy I have been vindicated and ordered reinstated with back pay," Attiah told Fox News Digital. "But in the meantime, I just wanted to put on a pretty gold dress, vibe to Rihanna’s music and eat cake! I wanted to be as loud about the win as possible so that other journalists will not be afraid to speak the truth." Attiah said her post was inspired by a video she liked from her party and "wanted to show that I take celebrating this huge win — for me, the Guild [the Washington Post union] and for journalism — very seriously!" It remains unclear whether she will formally return to work despite the arbitrator's order. A spokesperson for The Washington Post told Fox News Digital the paper respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further. TEACHERS WHO CELEBRATED CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION NOW CASH IN WITH TAXPAYER-FUNDED SETTLEMENTS Attiah sparked outrage last year for her posts about slain conservative icon Charlie Kirk on the liberal social media platform Bluesky following his assassination. "Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a White man that espoused violence is… not the same as violence," Attiah wrote at the time. In a separate post, she wrote, "Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for White men who espouse hatred and violence.’" Critics also slammed Attiah for misquoting Kirk in another post, attributing to him saying, "Black women do not have the brain processing power to be taken seriously. You have to go steal a White person's slot." On a July 2023 episode of "The Charlie Kirk Show," Kirk actually said, "If we would have said three weeks ago [...] that Joy Reid and Michelle Obama, and Sheila Jackson Lee, and Ketanji Brown Jackson were affirmative-action picks, we would have been called racist. But now they're comin' out and they're saying it for us! They're comin' out, and they're saying, 'I'm only here because of affirmative action.' Yeah, we know. You do not have the brain processing power to otherwise be taken really seriously. You had to go steal a White person's slot to go be taken somewhat seriously." TENNESSEE UNIVERSITY TO PAY PROFESSOR $1.9M AFTER CALLING CHARLIE KIRK A 'DISGUSTING PSYCHOPATH' Following the backlash, Attiah revealed she had been fired by the Post, saying in a termination letter her posts were "unacceptable" and "gross misconduct." Attiah filed a legal challenge against the Post over her termination last fall, and previously announced in June that she and the paper would enter arbitration.
